title: Ulyana and the Confession
premise: Ulyana Sterling, a night dispatcher whose hobby of reading police scanners has quietly solved three 'accidental' deaths, receives twin letters: one a full confession to a murder, one promising a second death within thirty days. The letters reference a taxi company ledger she realizes has been hiding coded entries in plain sight for years — a record of payoffs, silencings, and names. As she decodes it, she discovers the confessor is someone inside her own dispatch loop, killing to expose a cover-up the police themselves buried. The second letter's promised victim turns out to be Ulyana herself, the last living link to the original crime; in the end she chooses to publish the decoded ledger rather than save the confessor, trading one life for a justice the law refused to deliver.
about_author: Lior Thackeray spent a decade working overnight shifts in municipal transit before turning to crime fiction, a background that gives the book its insomnia-accurate texture of radio static and empty streets. The author lives in a coastal city and is known for refusing interviews, saying only that 'the best confessions happen at 3 a.m.'

chapters.title: The Quiet Hours
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A routine night dispatching taxis establishes her world: the radio chatter, the city's small crimes, and her private file of three 'accidents' she quietly disproved. The beat is controlled loneliness — competence as a substitute for connection.

chapters.title: Twin Envelopes
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Two letters arrive at the dispatch office, hand-addressed: one confessing to the drowning of a councilman's aide, one promising 'a second confession, in person, before the month ends.' The emotional beat is a jolt of recognition — she knows the victim's name from her own file.

chapters.title: What the Scanner Missed
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, with a flashback to her first solved death. She reopens her notes and finds the aide's accident report contains the same anomaly she spotted before: a taxi logged to a street with no fare. She realizes the letters' author knows her work intimately. Beat: dread mixed with flattery.

chapters.title: The Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Auditing old dispatch ledgers, she notices columns of fares that don't reconcile — coded entries hidden among routine trips. The beat is the thrill of the hunt, undercut when she finds her own shift supervisor's initials in the margin.

chapters.title: Detective Okafor
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. A weary detective who once dismissed Ulyana's anonymous tips is assigned the aide's reopened case. He half-remembers her voice from the tip line. The beat is institutional skepticism beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Fares That Never Existed
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She maps the coded entries and finds they cluster around dates of deaths and disappearances spanning fifteen years. The ledger isn't a killer's trophy — it's a payoff record. Beat: vertigo as a hobby becomes a conspiracy.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signs for Everything
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She tails the company's operations manager, Marcus Vey, whose initials authorize every anomalous entry. Watching him, she sees him burn a document in a barrel behind the depot. Beat: cold fear replacing curiosity.

chapters.title: Second Letter's Logic
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She analyzes the second letter's phrasing and realizes the 'second confession' will be a killing, and the promised victim is someone who can read the ledger — meaning her. Beat: the hunter understands she is the quarry.

chapters.title: Night Ride
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor takes an unmarked cab and, by chance, is dispatched by Ulyana. Their first face-to-face conversation, all subtext, ends with him leaving her his card. Beat: two loners recognizing each other's obsession.

chapters.title: The Confessor's Voice
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A third letter arrives — no confession, just a phone number and a time. She calls; the voice is disguised but uses dispatch jargon only insiders use. The confessor claims to be killing to force the buried case open. Beat: seduction of a shared cause.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor digs into the original case the ledger points to: a whistleblower at the taxi company who died in a 'gas leak' in 2009, investigated by a detective who later made captain. Beat: the rot goes up the chain.

chapters.title: The Captain's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She decodes the final cipher layer: the ledger's true author isn't Vey but retired Captain Aldous Renner, now a city safety commissioner. The company was the payment conduit. Beat: the scale of the cover-up lands.

chapters.title: Someone in the Loop
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She narrows the confessor to current or former dispatchers who'd know her habits. Suspicion poisons her relationships with coworkers; she can't tell ally from threat. Beat: paranoia isolating the investigator.

chapters.title: Dead Drop at Pier Nine
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The confessor arranges a meeting; she goes armed with a recorder. She sees a figure, is warned off by headlights — Vey watching — and flees with a partial glimpse: a dispatch headset hanging from the stranger's neck. Beat: near-miss terror.

chapters.title: Okafor's Bargain
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor confronts his own captain about Renner and is threatened with suspension. He chooses to work off the books with Ulyana. Beat: the law's agent goes outlaw, mirroring the theme.

chapters.title: The Name in the Margin
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Cross-referencing shift rosters with the letters' handwriting, she identifies the confessor: Dana Kovic, a dispatcher who worked the night the whistleblower died and has been waiting fifteen years. Beat: pity — the killer is a mirror of herself.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Confession
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Ulyana confronts Dana, who confesses fully: she has been killing the cover-up's foot soldiers to force the case into the open, and the 'second confession' is Renner — she intends to kill him and die trying. Beat: moral crisis, the price of survival.

chapters.title: Twenty-Nine Days
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor learns Renner has scheduled a 'safety audit' at the depot — Dana's chosen ground. He and Ulyana have hours, not days. Beat: the clock finally audible.

chapters.title: The Depot
chapters.summary: Alternating Ulyana/Okafor POV. Climax: Dana ambushes Renner at the depot; Ulyana intervenes, Okafor arrives; Vey, exposed and desperate, tries to burn the original ledger. In the chaos Dana is shot saving Ulyana, mortally wounding herself by choice. Beat: everything converges.

chapters.title: What Justice Costs
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Dana dies holding the decoded ledger, asking Ulyana to finish it 'outside the room.' Renner is arrested but the department begins burying the case. Beat: grief and the bitter arithmetic of survival.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Ulyana and Okafor's POV. They bypass the department: Ulyana mails the full decoded ledger to every newsroom, and Okafor resigns to testify as a civilian witness. Renner falls; Vey turns state's evidence. Beat: justice achieved by refusing the legal system's gatekeeping.

chapters.title: Night Shift, Again
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, epilogue. Weeks later, Ulyana is back on dispatch, the scanner murmuring. A new letter arrives — not a confession, but a thank-you, unsigned, from someone else who reads the night. She files it, and keeps listening. Beat: quiet, watchful peace with an open door.
